sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Luxor** ​(*luxor*) — ‌The ‌Palaces, the ​Southern Sanctuary ​· ​The palaces ​— ​belongs to ‌the ​Egyptian tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued under ‌the ​domain "Temple, ‌Thebes, ​Amun". The ​name ​means "The ​palaces"[^1].

​**Luxor** — ‌Arabic ‘the ​palaces’ ‌— names ​the ‌southern sanctuary ​of ‌the Theban ​triad, ‌where Amun ​visited in ​the ‌great Opet ‌festival ‌to renew ​his ​generative power. ‌Its ​ancient name, ​Ipet-resyt, ‘the ‌Southern ​Select Place’, ​marks ‌it as ​Karnak’s ‌counterpart across ​the ​river: not ​the god’s ​estate ‌but his ‌bridal-chamber.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the ​name as ​**Luxor** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/luxor/). ​The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ​description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form ​itself. The ‌plain ​ASCII form ​*luxor* ​survives as ‌a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the ‌early domain-name ​system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this ​name; ​**Luxor** is ​a ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​of the ‌reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. ​Etymologically the ‌name ​means ​"The ​palaces"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form ‌*luxor* ​survives ‌only because ​the ‌early ​domain-name ‌system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; ​it ‌is a ‌technological ‌compromise, ​not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The ​Unicode ‌restoration ​**Luxor** recovers ​the ‌full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ​scholarly ​transliteration ​directly ‌in the ‌address ​bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ​the ‌displayed ​form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**l** → ​**L** ‌— ​Same, ​capitalized
- ​**u** → ‌**u** ​— ‌Same
- ​**x** → ‌**x** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**o** → ​**o** ​— ​Same
- ​**r** ‌→ **r** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
**Luxor** ​— ‌Arabic ‘the ‌palaces’ ​— ​names the ​southern ​sanctuary ​of ‌the Theban ​triad, ​where ‌Amun visited ​in ‌the ​great ‌Opet festival ​to ​renew ​his generative ​power. ​Its ‌ancient ​name, Ipet-resyt, ‌‘the ​Southern ‌Select Place’, ​marks ‌it ​as ‌Karnak’s counterpart ​across ​the ‌river: not ‌the ‌god’s ​estate ​but his ‌bridal-chamber.[^1]

### ​The ​Southern Sanctuary

‌Ipet-resyt ​— ​the ‌harem-temple where ​Amun’s ‌fertility ​was ​renewed each ​year.

### ​The ‌Birth Colonnade

‌Reliefs ​of ‌the ​divine birth ​of ‌Amenhotep ‌III — ‌the ‌king’s ​theology ‌of legitimate ​succession.

### ​The ​Colonnade of ‌Amenhotep ​III

​Fourteen ​massive papyrus ‌columns ​— ​the finest ​preserved ‌New ​Kingdom ‌colonnade.

### Opet’s ​Destination

‌The ​river-end of ‌the ‌great ​festival: ​Amun’s barque ​docked ​here ‌for the ‌marriage-renewal ​rites.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Luxor’s mythology ​is the fertility-cycle ‌of Amun himself: ‌each year the ​god sailed south ​from Karnak to ​his harem at ​Ipet-resyt, married his ​own power in ‌the sanctuary, and ​returned renewed. The ​temple’s birth-colonnade extends ‌the cycle to ​kingship — Amenhotep ‌III’s divine conception ​carved as theology-in-stone.[^1]

### ‌The Southern Journey ​(Opet Festival)

The ​Opet festival’s climax ​was the god’s ​arrival at Ipet-resyt: ​the barque of ‌Amun moored before ​the colonnade, the ‌Theban crowd celebrating ​the union that ‌renewed the Nile, ​the king, and ‌the year in ​a single night ‌of liturgy. The ​return to Karnak ​closed the cycle ‌eleven days later.[^2]

### ‌Amun and Mutemwiya ‌(Divine Birth)

Luxor’s ​colonnade reliefs narrate ​the conception of ‌Amenhotep III: Amun ​takes the form ​of the king, ‌visits queen Mutemwiya, ​the child is ​fashioned by Khnum ‌on the ​potter’s wheel and ‌blessed by the ​gods — the ​canonical statement that ​the pharaoh is ​the god’s literal ‌son, carved at ‌full scale.

### The ​Sanctuary Continuous (The ‌Mosque of Abu ​Haggag)

A mosque ​still stands inside ‌the temple’s court ‌— Abu Haggag ‌of Luxor, whose ‌mouloud festival each ​year crowds the ‌ancient colonnade with ​boats and lights. ​The building has ​never stopped being ‌sacred; only the ​name of the ​sacred changed, from ​Ipet-resyt to the ‌Sheikh’s mosque.

### The ​Palaces (Modern Name)

​The Arabs who ​settled among the ‌ruins called them ​*al-uqsur* — ‘the ‌castles’ — seeing ​palaces in the ‌pylons; the name ​shrank to Luxor ‌and became the ‌city’s. It is ​one of the ​few cases where ​the medieval name ​of the ruins ‌replaced the ancient ‌name of the ​living town.
